title: The styles of recitation
hook: several authentic readings, passed down in chains of reciters

segments.voice: Yesterday, tafsir: explaining the Qur'an, its own verses speaking first. Your line was the book explains itself. Did you let someone explain themselves? Day three hundred twenty-two, the end of a week.

In Medina, Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a man named Hisham reciting Surah al-Furqan in the prayer, and some of the words came out differently from the way Umar had learned them from the Prophet himself. Umar was so upset he could barely wait for the prayer to end. When it did, he took Hisham by his cloak and marched him straight to the Prophet ﷺ. Today: the styles of recitation.
screen: `SAME SURAH, DIFFERENT WORDS.` → `UMAR COULD BARELY WAIT.` → `MARCHED TO THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: The Prophet asked Hisham to recite. Then he said: this is how it was revealed. He asked Umar to recite. And he said again: this is how it was revealed. Then he explained that the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, seven modes, so recite whichever is easy for you. The story is in Bukhari. Scholars have discussed for centuries exactly what the seven ahruf were, and there's no single agreed answer. But within those permitted ways stand what are called the qira'at, the readings. Each is a way of reciting the same Qur'an, passed from teacher to student in an unbroken chain back to the Prophet. The differences are small: a vowel, a letter, how long a sound is held. In al-Fatiha, for instance, some readers recite maliki yawm al-din, King of the Day, and others maaliki, Owner of the Day. Both are accepted, and both are true of God. In the tenth century, a scholar in Baghdad, Ibn Mujahid, set out seven famous readers; later scholars recognized ten. Each has two main transmitters, whose names identify the reading. Today most of the world recites in the reading of Hafs from Asim. Across much of North and West Africa, you'll hear Warsh from Nafi'. Muslims don't treat these as rival versions. They're held to be the Qur'an itself, recited in the ways the Prophet taught. Many voices, one text. Now look back at the week. Abu Bakr's collection gathered it. Uthman's copies spread it. Dots and vowels helped new readers. Arabic, and translation. Pickthall and the 1934 translation. Tafsir, explaining it. And now the readings: the living voice under the page.
screen: `UMAR AND HISHAM` · `THIS IS HOW IT WAS REVEALED` · `MALIKI AND MAALIKI` · `HAFS, WARSH AND THE TEN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to two reciters. After the bell, find al-Fatiha recited by two different people, perhaps one in the reading of Hafs and one in Warsh, and listen for what changes and what doesn't. For now, sit and remember a voice you've heard reciting: in a mosque, a video, a relative's kitchen. Hear it in your mind. Then picture another voice, somewhere else in the world, reciting the same surah at this same moment. The bell holds the time.
Qira'at. The readings: accepted ways of reciting the same Qur'an, each passed down in a chain of teachers back to the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: many voices, one text. Today, when you hear something familiar said in an unfamiliar accent or way, listen for what's the same underneath. Day three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Most Muslims recite in the reading of Hafs from Asim, many in North and West Africa in Warsh from Nafi', and specialist reciters learn several readings from teachers with a chain of transmission back to the Prophet.

fork.setup: you're Umar. you've marched a man to the Prophet for reciting a surah differently from you. what does the Prophet say?
options: both of you recited it as it was revealed.
fork.reveal: 'this is how it was revealed', to both. the Qur'an came in seven modes: recite whichever is easy for you.

original.note: Arabic: readings, the accepted ways of reciting the Qur'an. from the same root as Qur'an.

trapdoor: what you thought: different styles of chanting the Qur'an.
what it means: accepted readings with small differences of vowel and letter, each passed down in a chain to the Prophet.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Mujahid's seven, the later ten, two transmitters each, and the old question of how they relate to the seven ahruf.
